issues.legal_issue: Government ghatwali tenures fall within legislation that expressly includes ghatwali tenures, notwithstanding that some compensation-calculation or payment provisions may not apply to them.
material_facts: The appellants held Government ghatwali tenures governed by a special regulation.
The land-reform legislation expressly included ghatwali tenures and ghatwals in its definitions.
The appellants relied on provisions for calculating net income and paying compensation that they argued could not apply to their tenures.
issues.conclusion: The Government ghatwali tenures were within the legislation and could be acquired under it; the possible inapplicability of particular compensation provisions did not exclude them.
issues.legal_principle: The express inclusion of a category in an artificial statutory definition is not cut down by the ordinary meaning of the defined term absent compelling reasons. Provisions addressing particular deductions or the manner of compensation payment do not exclude a tenure from the statute merely because they may not apply to it. The Court considered sections 2(o), 2(q), 2(r), 23(1)(f), and 32(4) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950.

predicates.tenure_acquisition_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether legislation authorizes acquisition of a ghatwali tenure held by a government ghatwal.
predicates.legislation_expressly_includes_ghatwali_: The legislature expressly includes ghatwali tenures and ghatwals within the relevant statutory definitions.
predicates.some_compensation_provisions_do_not_appl: Some provisions governing deductions from income or the manner of compensation payment do not apply to the tenure.
predicates.all_compensation_provisions_apply: The provisions governing deductions from income and the manner of compensation payment apply to the tenure.

issues.definition: When an acquisition dispute concerns a government ghatwali tenure and the legislation expressly includes ghatwali tenures, the tenure remains within the acquisition law whether or not some compensation provisions apply.

issues.legal_issue: State legislation whose substance is the acquisition of property does not become legislation on national defence or the armed forces merely because the affected tenures carry duties of a quasi-military character.
material_facts: The appellants argued that their ghatwali tenures had a quasi-military character and that legislation applying to them concerned matters reserved to the Union.
The legislation provided for the transfer of ownership of estates to the State.
The Court noted that quasi-military ghatwali duties had largely lost their importance and were rarely demanded.
issues.conclusion: The legislation concerned acquisition of property, fell within the State legislative field, and was not outside the State Legislature’s competence by reason of the Union subjects of defence or armed forces.
issues.legal_principle: Legislative competence is determined by the pith and substance of the law. A law whose substance is acquisition of property falls within Entry 36 of List II and is not legislation on Entries 1 or 2 of List I merely because the property is associated with quasi-military duties. The Court followed The State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga and Others, [1952] S.C.R. 898.

predicates.legislative_competence_challenge: The proceeding challenges whether a state legislature had authority to enact a law affecting the tenure.
predicates.law_transfers_ownership_of_property: The law’s substance is the transfer of ownership of property to the state.
predicates.tenure_duties_are_not_substantially_defe: The duties associated with the tenure are not, in substance, matters of national defence or the armed forces of the Union.

issues.definition: A state legislature is competent to enact a law transferring property ownership when the law’s substance is property acquisition and the associated tenure duties are not substantially matters of national defence or the Union’s armed forces.

issues.legal_issue: A special regulation governing a particular tenure does not prevent a later property-acquisition law from applying to that tenure when the acquisition law expressly covers it and provides for vesting despite other laws.
material_facts: The appellants’ tenures were governed by a special regulation concerning ghatwali tenures.
The later land-reform legislation expressly included ghatwali tenures and provided for vesting upon notification notwithstanding other laws.
The appellants argued that a general land-reform law did not affect the special regulation and tenures governed by it.
issues.conclusion: The special-law principle did not prevent acquisition under the Act, and no question of repealing the special regulation arose.
issues.legal_principle: The special-law-over-general-law principle did not apply because the legislation in pith and substance concerned acquisition of property and expressly included the tenures, providing for vesting notwithstanding other laws. The Court applied Raja Suriya Pal Singh v. The State of U.P. and Another, [1952] S.C.R. 1056, and held that a prior grant or special legal regime cannot prevent a competent legislature from legislating within its authority.

predicates.special_tenure_acquisition_dispute: The proceeding concerns acquisition of a tenure governed by a special legal regime.
predicates.acquisition_law_expressly_covers_the_ten: The acquisition law expressly includes the category of tenure at issue.
predicates.law_provides_vesting_despite_other_laws: The law provides for vesting of the tenure despite provisions in other laws.

issues.definition: When an acquisition dispute concerns a specially regulated tenure that the acquisition law expressly covers, a provision for vesting despite other laws means the special regulation does not bar acquisition.
